name: North Buttress

pitch_detail.grade: Steep snow, with a dirty 5.6 bypass in late season
pitch_detail.notes: From the cirque camp, climb steep snow to the toe of the buttress at roughly 5,600 ft. The bergschrund here often forces a bypass on rock - reported as dirty 5.6 in September conditions, largely avoidable on snow in July.
Follow the couloir system toward the buttress crest. This is the rockfall funnel; move early and keep the party out of each other's fall line.
Traversing snowfields exposed to rockfall from the hanging glaciers above, with repeated snow-to-rock transitions and moats to negotiate as you gain the buttress proper.

The long body of the buttress: mostly Class 3, 4 and low 5th on the crest and its flanks. Route-finding is tricky and the protection is not always where you want it - expect runouts and be ready to build belays in imperfect rock.
The crux: a slabby step to the left near the ridge crest. The hardest climbing on the route and the reason to carry rock shoes.
An airy but technically easier traverse around the right side of the ridge above the crux.
A snow arete leads to the summit. Place a picket if the snow is firm; the arete is narrow and the exposure is total.

descent_text: The buttress is an ascent line only; the standard exit is over the top and down the other side. From the summit, downclimb the summit snowpatch (about 300 ft, 40 degrees at the base to nearly 50 degrees at the top - protect it with flukes or pickets, with the strongest climber first on belay) onto the Southeast Glacier, then descend the S-shaped snowfield past the bergschrund near 7,900 ft, keeping running belays where the gradient steepens and the runout is bad. Off the glacier, cross the rocky rib on the lower ledge, contour northeast through the talus basin, climb back up the heather chute to the northeast ridge crest, and follow the crest back over the terraced rock nose - one short rappel over the 25-ft step - to Luna Col. One traverse party instead descended the Southeast Glacier and continued toward Outrigger Peak and Picket Pass, which is the option if you are traversing the range rather than returning to Luna Col. Either way, a party that camped in Luna Cirque has to regain roughly 2,400 ft to Luna Col to retrieve gear and exit via Access Creek. Allow a full long day.
approach: Two very different ways in, both serious. The usual modern approach mirrors the Luna Col approach and then drops over the back: SR 20 to the Ross Dam trailhead, a mile of trail to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock, the Ross Lake Resort boat to Big Beaver Landing at about 1,600 ft, then 10-11.5 miles of Big Beaver Creek Trail past 39 Mile Camp to Luna Camp, another mile or so to the marked cut-off, a log crossing of Big Beaver Creek just north of Access Creek, and the Access Creek bushwhack (north bank through huckleberry, cross to the south bank near 3,800 ft where the brush pinches out) to Access Creek Basin at 4,300 ft. From there the scree chute to Access Col at 6,100 ft and the steep heather traverse to Luna Col at about 7,100-7,200 ft. From Luna Col descend north-northwest into Luna Cirque to Luna Lake at about 4,800 ft and continue southwest to a camp on the cirque floor beneath the buttress. The whole approach runs about 17 miles and 7,000 ft of gain from the Ross Lake water-taxi dock, and the descent from Luna Col into the cirque costs another 2,400 ft that has to be regained on the way out. Alan Kearney's party came in from the north instead, from Chilliwack Lake in Canada up the Chilliwack River Trail, over Whatcom Pass and across the Challenger Glacier before descending into Luna Cirque to camp at Luna Lake - a longer, higher and even more committing approach.
overview: A Beckey classic and one of the great long alpine lines of the Pickets: roughly 4,000 ft and about 20 pitches of mixed snow and rock rising out of Luna Cirque to East Fury's summit, mostly Class 3, 4 and low 5th with a single 5.9 crux and a snow arete finish.
beta: The route rises straight out of Luna Cirque above Lousy Lake on the north side of Fury, starting from around 5,600 ft near the cirque floor. Begin on steep snow, then work into a couloir system - a bergschrund at the base often forces a rock bypass, and in late season that bypass has been reported as dirty 5.6 - and follow it toward the buttress crest, crossing snowfields exposed to rockfall from hanging glaciers above. Higher up, snow, rock and moats alternate and the route-finding is tricky, with protection not always where you want it; near the crest a slabby step of about 5.9 is the technical crux, after which an airy but easier traverse around the right side of the ridge leads to a snow arete running to the summit. One party reached the ridge crest in about 4.5 hours from a camp at 4,000 ft in Luna Cirque. Alan Kearney, who repeated it in September 1992 with Mark Price, noted that the late season made for much more rock climbing down low, since Beckey and Davis in July 1962 climbed a lot of snow and avoided most of the rock.
gear: 60 m double ropes or a single 60 m plus tag line
steep snow tool plus ice axe
bivy gear for a possible forced bivouac
fa: Fred Beckey and Dan Davis, July 1962
face: North Buttress, above Luna Cirque and Lousy Lake
